Rethinking OCT AI at Cleveland Clinic: Practical Lessons in Local Foundation Model Training, Targeted Disease Adaptation, and Better Segmentation of Complex Retinal Pathology

Cristian Barrera · Cole Eye Institute, Cleveland Clinic · AI Summit 2026

We are building an OCT segmentation pipeline that runs entirely inside the institution: model development, experiment tracking and deployment on four local GPUs, with no paid managed services and no patient data leaving the building.

The backbone is VisionFM, a ViT-B/16 model pretrained with iBOT, which we carried forward by continued pretraining on 3.2 million OCT B-scans. On top of it we train segmentation heads for sixteen retinal layer and fluid targets, adapt them per disease cohort, and test a mixture-of-experts block as an alternative to training a separate model per task. Every run is tracked in MLflow and exported to ONNX for serving.

The point of the work is not a single benchmark number. It is that a hospital research group can build, track, adapt and deploy this class of model on its own hardware, and that the practical lessons - which metric to optimise, when a model is quietly declining to answer, what a routing diagnostic does and does not tell you - transfer to other groups trying the same thing.

Figures

Limitations, stated plainly

These are preliminary results from work in progress, and the honest reading matters more than the headline. In particular:

Results are preliminary and internal.

Every accuracy number here comes from internal validation sets. Nothing has been through a broad external test.

The validation split was not grouped by patient.

Splits were made at the B-scan level, so scans from the same eye can appear on both sides of the split. The F1 values should be read as optimistic, and they are not a substitute for a held-out patient-level test. Re-baselining on a grouped split is in progress.

The reference annotations were produced by correcting the previous system's output.

That system is therefore partly evaluated against its own corrected output, which flatters it on some structures and makes a clean head-to-head comparison impossible. We make no claim of superiority over it on accuracy. Establishing one needs blinded annotation drawn from scratch.

Dice and F1 are the wrong metrics for a one-pixel boundary.

A two-pixel shift can move Dice a long way while the boundary remains clinically fine. Our evaluation is moving to boundary error in microns, which is the field standard and is what Figure 2 reports.

The mixture-of-experts contribution has not been isolated.

The only matched on/off comparison we have shows no measurable difference, and the two runs did not share a split. The routing figures describe what the gate learns; they are not evidence that it helps.

What comes next

  1. Test on external, held-out cohorts.
  2. Repeat the mixture-of-experts ablation on a fixed, patient-grouped split.
  3. Train a joint multi-layer head, so anatomical ordering can be enforced structurally rather than hoped for.
  4. Train an OCT foundation model of our own rather than continuing to adapt VisionFM.

Further reading

How a vision transformer sees an OCT B-scan — a design note on why patch size is the constraint that drives everything else: one 16-pixel patch spans 62 microns of depth, which is thicker than the ellipsoid zone, the external limiting membrane and the retinal pigment epithelium put together. It also sets out why Dice misleads on a one-pixel boundary.

That note describes the newer single-target line of work, which does use low-rank adapters on the encoder. The sixteen models in Figure 3 above do not — there the encoder is frozen and only the decoder is trained. Same backbone, different recipe.
